case_name: Sir Mortimer B. Davis—Jewish General Hospital c. P.S.
text:
Sir Mortimer B. Davis—Jewish
General Hospital c. P.S.

2014 QCCS 1355

JJ0379

COUR SUPÉRIEURE

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

N° :

500-17-080829-149

DATE
:

2 avril 2014

______________________________________________________________________

PRESIDENT : THE HONOURABLE
DENIS JACQUES, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

SIR MORTIMER B. DAVIS –
JEWISH GENERAL HOSPITAL AND

DR. JOSEPH PORTNOY

Petitioners

v.

P. S.

Respondent

and

M. SZ.

Mise en cause

and

LE CURATEUR PUBLIC DU QUÉBEC

Mis en cause

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

on a motion for
authorization of medical treatment

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

The petitioners, the Sir Mortimer B. Davis -
Jewish General Hospital “the Hospital” and Dr. Joseph Portnoy, its director of
professional services, present a motion for authorization for forced placement,
treatment and medication of the respondent, Mr. P. S..

[
2
]

Mr. S., who is currently hospitalized in the
intensive care psychiatric unit of the Hospital, refuses the treatment
requested by the petitioners. He wants to go back home with his family and
start working again.

[
3
]

This motion raises the application of
sections
4
,
11
,
12
,
15
,
16
and
23
of the
Civil Code of Quebec
, which read as
follows:

4.
Every person is fully able to exercise his civil rights.

In certain cases, the law provides
for representation or assistance.

11.
No person may be made to undergo care of any nature, whether
for examination, specimen taking, removal of tissue, treatment or any other
act, except with his consent.

If the person concerned is
incapable of giving or refusing his consent to care, a person authorized by law
or by mandate given in anticipation of his incapacity may do so in his place.

12.
A
person who gives his consent to or refuses care for another person is bound to
act in the sole interest of that person, taking into account, as far as
possible, any wishes the latter may have expressed.

If he gives his consent, he shall
ensure that the care is beneficial notwithstanding the gravity and permanence
of certain of its effects, that it is advisable in the circumstances and that
the risks incurred are not disproportionate to the anticipated benefit.

15.
Where
it is ascertained that a person of full age is incapable of giving consent to
care required by his or her state of health, consent is given by his or her
mandatory, tutor or curator. If the person of full age is not so represented,
consent is given by his or her married, civil union or
de facto
spouse
or, if the person has no spouse or his or her spouse is prevented from giving
consent, it is given by a close relative or a person who shows a special interest
in the person of full age.

16.
The
authorization of the court is necessary where the person who may give consent
to care required by the state of health of a minor or a person of full age who
is incapable of giving his consent is prevented from doing so or, without
justification, refuses to do so; it is also required where a person of full age
who is incapable of giving his consent categorically refuses to receive care,
except in the case of hygienic care or emergency.

The authorization of the court is
necessary, furthermore, to cause a minor 14 years of age or over to undergo
care he refuses, except in the case of emergency if his life is in danger or
his integrity threatened, in which case the consent of the person having
parental authority or the tutor is sufficient.

23.
When
the court is called upon to rule on an application for authorization with
respect to care or the alienation of a body part, it obtains the opinions of
experts, of the person having parental authority, of the mandatory, of the tutor
or the curator and of the tutorship council; it may also obtain the opinion of
any person who shows a special interest in the person concerned by the
application.

The court is also bound to obtain
the opinion of the person concerned unless that is impossible, and to respect
his refusal unless the care is required by his state of health.

[
4
]

The legislator did not provide in the
Code

the applicable criteria to determine the incapacity of a person to consent to
medical care.

[
5
]

In
Institut Philippe-Pinel de Montréal
c.

G. (A.)
[1]
, the Court of appeal examines different tests, including the one
prescribed in the
Hospitals Act of Nova Scotia
[2]
:

[49] […] In determining
whether or not a person is capable of consenting to treatment the examining
psychiatrist shall consider whether or not the person being examined:

a)

understands the condition for which the treatment is proposed;

b)

understands the nature and purpose of the treatment;

c)

understands the risks involved in undergoing the treatment;

d)

understands the risks involved in not undergoing the treatment; and

e)

whether or not his ability to consent is affected by his condition.

[
6
]

Commenting the tests, the Court of appeal puts
an emphasis on two criteria which are first, the understanding by the patient
of his condition and secondly, the effects of his condition on his capacity to
consent to treatment:

[54] Tous ces tests ont des traits communs.
Ceux qui incluent, entre autres, les deux critères suivants sont plus
complets : la perception de sa maladie par la personne impliquée et les
effets de cette maladie sur sa capacité de consentir à des soins.

[55] En santé mentale, il y a une réalité
extrêmement importante : la personne impliquée se rend-elle compte qu’elle
est malade? C’est un critère capital, à l’égard duquel le profane est vulnérable
parce qu’il risque d’être manipulé par la personne malade qui, sous d’autres
aspects, paraît normale et peut même ébahir. L’ignorance ou la
non-reconnaissance par une personne de sa maladie est trop souvent la
composante essentielle du maintien de cette maladie.

[56] Il faut, de plus, vérifier si l’inaptitude
à consentir n’est pas inhérente à l’affection d’une personne. Ce constat est
facile en cas de trouble mental sévère; il l’est moins dans des situations plus
nuancées.

[57] Cela ne veut pas dire pour autant que les
critères ne doivent pas être considérés dans leur ensemble; une attention
particulière doit, cependant, être apportée aux deux mentionnés ci-dessus.

[
7
]

Mr. S. was currently living with his wife and
three children X, 21 years old, Y, 19 and Z, 13.

[
8
]

He owns a taxi, works as a taxi driver and also
receives incomes from rental properties he owns.

[
9
]

He is presently 62 years of age and was admitted
to the Jewish General Hospital on December 17
th
, 2013.

[
10
]

Mr. S. has a significant psychiatrist history.

[
11
]

In his initial report dated January 20, 2014,
his treating psychiatrist, Dr. Robert Biskin notes:

His primary diagnoses are
dependant
personality disorder
,
major depressive disorder, and benzodiazepine
dependence
. His first admission at the Jewish General Hospital was in 1971
with a diagnosis of “borderline syndrome”. He was admitted another 7 times to
psychiatry between 2011 and the present, including his current admission, and
was also admitted to a medical unit once following a suicide attempt.

Mr. S. has a
history of multiple
suicide attempts
with the
first attempt
that is recorded in the
hospital charts occurring in
March 2011
. At the time he cut his wrists
and took a Tylenol overdose and then showed these injuries to his wife and
daughter. He has subsequently made
at least 2 serious and nearly lethal
suicide attempts by overdosing on approximately 60 tablets of Tylenol in April
2011 and September 2013. He has also had over 20 visits to the emergency room
at the JGH since 2011 for suicidal thoughts, anxiety, and ongoing depressive
symptoms
.

Mr. S. has been actively followed
in the JGH Department of Psychiatry for the past year by Dr. Biskin and Dr.
Davis. He has been treated with many different medications for depression and
anxiety although he has a history of partial to complete
non-adherence with
most medications
, other than Ativan, which he has used at gradually
increasing doses. Unfortunately, none of the medications have been dramatic
benefit and Mr. S.’s symptoms continue to worsen. During his outpatient
follow-up, Mr. S. would also repeatedly miss initial evaluations and follow-up
appointments. He has been given psycho-education and brief psychotherapy for
other means of managing his distress in crisis but he demonstrates an inability
to follow through on these strategies. One outpatient appointment with Dr.
Biskin was jointly attended by Mr. S. and his wife, although this meeting was
not very productive.

Our
underlining

[
12
]

On December 17, 2013, Mr. S. had a fourth
suicide attempt and, since then, is hospitalized at the Jewish General
Hospital.

[
13
]

In his report, Dr. Biskin describes Mr. S.’s
last suicidal attempt:

Mr. S. is currently hospitalized at
the JGH since December 17, 2013 following a suicide attempt. Approximately one
week prior to his admission at the JGH Mr. S. was having a discussion with his
wife that he found very upsetting and which triggered sudden thoughts of
suicide. He then went to the basement of his house and
started cutting his
wrists with the intent to die
.
He cut his left wrist several times and
his wife then came downstairs. On seeing her, he did not stop harming himself
and continued to cut his wrist and also stabbed himself in the stomach
approximately 12 times
. His wife then woke their 19 year old son who was
also at home and had him call for an ambulance. Mr. S. was brought to the
Montreal General Hospital and his wrist was surgically repaired as he cut a
tendon and a nerve. An exploratory laparotomy revealed that he did not puncture
any organs or major blood vessels in his abdomen. After recovering from the
surgery he was transferred to the Jewish General Hospital department of
psychiatry and has been hospitalized on a closed unit since then.

Our
underlining

[
14
]

Dr. Biskin identifies three major stressors that
triggered the current and previous suicide attempts.

[
15
]

First, the financial strain under which the
family is standing.

[
16
]

A second major stressor for Mr. S. is the mental
health of his 20 year old son and the intervention of the DPJ regarding his 13
year old daughter.

[
17
]

A third major stressor is the relation with his
wife who pushes him to work long hours and minimizes his condition and
diagnosis.

[
18
]

In his January report, Dr. Biskin concludes on
those terms to request the present order:

Mr. S.’s current clinical
situation is extremely serious
. His diagnoses are
major depressive disorder, severe and recurrent, benzodiazepine dependence, and
dependent personality disorder. Over the past year he has made multiple
increasingly lethal suicide attempts that have always been in the context of
familial discord. This is clearly not safe for him and
the likelihood of
future suicide attempts and future completed suicide is very high
.
His
home situation is very difficult and is not allowing him to recover from his
psychiatric illnesses, if not worsening the situation
. Returning to his
family home is extremely likely to lead to continuation or progressive
worsening of his symptoms and further suicide attempts.
Due to these risks
and lack of insight
, we are requesting a treatment order to ensure a period
of increased stability to allow proper recovery and insight into his
difficulties.

In light of these risks, we are
making the following recommendations:

That Mr. S. takes medications as
prescribed by his treating psychiatrist.

That Mr. S. lives in a setting
approved of by the treatment team.

That Mr. S. continues to be
followed in our outpatient department.

This treatment plan be in effect
for a period of 12 months in order to allow a period of stability that will
lead to improved safety, functioning, judgment, and insight.

Our
underlining

[
19
]

Before the first hearing held on February 19
th
,
Dr. Biskin prepared an update after his first January report, which was signed
on February 14
th
, 2014.

[
20
]

In his update, even if an improvement occurred,
Dr. Biskin states that Mr. S.’s insight remains very poor:

With regards to his family
situation, Mr. S. reports daily that he wants to return home and return to work
immediately. He also states that he promises he will never make another suicide
attempt, which is a promise he has made in the past as well.

(…)

Mr. S.’s insight into his
current situation and the stressors remains very poor
.
Many of the stressors that led to the most recent suicide
attempt and many of the other suicide attempts over the past three years remain
unchanged
. His financial situation is, to the best of our knowledge, as
tenuous as prior although he frequently reports some income from some of his
properties. Offers to set up further meetings with the community service that
has financial experts are refused.
The mental health of his family is also
likely unchanged
, although Mr. S. reports that all his children are feeling
better. He has also reported that
the Department of Youth Protection has
again become involved with regards to his youngest daughter
. Nonetheless,
Mr. S. is convinced that after his current treatment in the hospital he is safe
and ready to return home and he believes that he is not at any risk of
worsening depressive symptoms and he believes that he is not at risk of
suicidal thoughts returning.
His poor insight into his own situation is a
very worrisome
.

(…)

His judgment remains poor
regarding what can be done to change his situation

as he focuses solely on repeating things that he has tried before and is unable
or unwilling to focus on anything else. Insight is similarly impaired with
regards to awareness of his illness, how to treat his illness, typical duration
to recovery and risks of relapse.
His insight is best described as
superficial with no awareness of how his life and stressors in his life affect
his mental health
.

Our
underlining

[
21
]

In his February update, Dr. Biskin still
concludes to the necessity of the treatment order:

In summary, Mr. S. continues to
pose a serious risk to his own life due to his diagnoses of major depressive
disorder, severe and in early partial remission, dependent personality
disorder, and benzodiazepine dependence
. His
history of non-compliance with treatment and returning to the same environment
and stressors that have triggered many previous suicide attempts and suicidal
thoughts prevent proper recovery. In particular, the major risk is returning to
his home environment at it is highly stressful and has repeatedly been
identified as the major factor leading to suicidal behaviour. Mr. S. has
consistently demonstrated an inhability to make changes in his home environment
or to leave this environment, which puts him at such high risk.
Due to these
risks and lack of insight
, we are requesting a treatment order to ensure a
period of increased stability to allow proper recovery and insight into his
difficulties.

Our
underlining

[
22
]

At the February 19
th
hearing, after
the evidence was closed, Mr. S.’s lawyer required a reopening of the inquiry to
present an expert and the testimony of Mrs. M. (Sz.) S., Mr. S.’s wife.

[
23
]

No objection was raised by the Hospital and the
motion to reopen the hearing was accepted. An interim order was then pronounced
by the Court to apply the conclusions requested by the Hospital, until judgment
on the Hospital’s original motion.

[
24
]

On March 26
th
, the Court received the
report and heard the testimony of Dr. Ginette Lavoie, psychiatrist, presented
by Mr. S..

[
25
]

As she explained, Dr. Lavoie met Mr. S. at the
intensive care unit of the Hospital on February 28
th
, 2014, for a
period of about an hour and a half.

[
26
]

She concludes that Mr. S. is able to decide for
his treatment and residence.

[
27
]

The Court does not share her opinion.

[
28
]

It is obvious that the facts on which Dr. Lavoie
based her report are very incomplete.

[
29
]

Dr. Lavoie has seen Mr. S. only once, for a
short period of time and never met his family.

[
30
]

In her written report, Dr. Lavoie reports not
much about Mr. S.’s previous suicide attempts. Nothing about the cutting of the
wrists on two occasions. She also minimizes the suicidal attempt of December
2013, which she describes in these terms:

Le 17 décembre dernier, Monsieur
s’est infligé des blessures internes. Il tend à croire qu’il ne s’agissait pas
de blessures très importantes, plutôt superficielles, pour lesquelles il a tout
de même été hospitalisé. Ceci est survenu au moment où son fils revenait de
l’épicerie et qu’il avait été mis à la porte du IGA sans raison selon lui.
Monsieur rapporte toujours la difficulté de compréhension de ses enfants et de
sa femme par rapport à lui lorsqu’il se sent
‘frustré’
.

[
31
]

The reality is that, on that last incident, Mr. S.
opened his wrist and stabbed himself with a knife 12 times in the stomach, in
front of his wife, before being transported in ambulance to the Hospital.

[
32
]

Dr. Lavoie admits that Mr. S.’s condition is
directly influenced by the identified stressors (financial, youth protection,
relations with his wife) and that hospitalisation or group home with follow-up
might be the solution if those stressors are still present.

[
33
]

It is clear that all suicide attempts have
always been in a context of familial discord.

[
34
]

The evidence clearly shows that it would be very
dangerous to send Mr. S. back to his house at this time, with all those
stressors.

[
35
]

When asked about it, in her testimony at the
hearing, Dr. Lavoie had to admit that Mr. S., if sent back at those stressors,
would be at high risk. On a scale of five, she estimates the risk between four
to five.

[
36
]

The Court endorses the conclusions of the
medical team from the Jewish General Hospital.

[
37
]

The testimony of the treating social worker
Darlene Johnstone and the last update of treating psychiatrist Dr. Biskin are
clear and should be sustained.

[
38
]

In her written report, social worker Johnstone
states:

Mr. S. is repeatedly in ER at the
Jewish General Hospital with extreme anxiety and suicidal ideation or attempts.
He has had 22 ER visits since 2011 and six hospitalizations (five in psychiatry
and two in medicine, one following an overdose of Tylenol, the second provoking
this hospitalization, when he stabbed himself in the abdomen 12 times and cut
his wrist, damaging a tendon). Hospitalizations have ranged from one day to
several months. He has never benefitted from any hospitalization of any
duration, returning home to same difficult psychosocial situation and a
recurrence of his symptoms. He is highly unreliable with outpatient
appointments for no clear reason.

There have been multiple attempts
at family therapy for school refusal since the children were young but no
lasting changes. Currently his son is 20, his eldest daughter is 19 and his
youngest daughter is 13. Batshaw Youth and Family Services have been involved
on a repeated basis, both for school refusals on the part of his son and
youngest daughter and as a result of Mr. S.’s suicide attempts that have been
witnessed by the children including this most recent attempt.

Tensions between Mr. S. and his
wife are extremely high. Mr. S. describes regular bouts of both verbal and
physical abuse wherein his wife denigrates him in front of the children and
insists they do the same. She demands that he drive his taxi for 70-80 hours
per week to manage their bills. They have substantial debt, including owing a
large sum of money to the children, from whom they have borrowed. During his
admission in November 2013 he presented with facial injuries after being beaten
by his son and injuries on his legs from his wife kicking him.

[
39
]

And Mrs. Johnstone concludes:

In light of this continuous
pattern, the seriousness of his suicide attempts, his escalating financial
problems and the frustration experienced by staff, whether in ER, on the ward
or in the community, Dr Biskin has arranged for a court hearing for Forced
placement. As well, a curatorship application is being deposited today for measures
«
provisoires
»
, and this writer will call the
Commission
des droits de la personne
.

[
40
]

At the last hearing on March 26
th
,
Dr. Biskin presented another update of his previous reports signed on January
20
th
and February 14
th
, 2014.

[
41
]

He explains that a meeting with Mr. S.’s wife
and his youngest daughter took place on March 19, 2014.

[
42
]

Dr. Biskin reports that Mr. S.’s goals for
family therapy are not shared by his wife, which would make family therapy
difficult. Mrs. S. insisted that medication alone and returning to work would
be what Mr. S. needs.

[
43
]

He explains that Mr. S. continues to have poor
insight into his situation and is still very fragile.

[
44
]

Mr. S.’s behaviour is directly influenced by the
identified stressors.

[
45
]

Another incident occurred on March 17, 2014, as
reported by Dr. Biskin in his report in these terms:

On March 17, 2014 Mr. S. received a
call from his wife in which he interpreted that there were increasing financial
problems. This led him to quickly return the same anxious and highly suicidal
state that he arrived in. He presented to the nurses stating that he wants to
die and required extra medication to settle down. After talking to his wife
again and realizing he misinterpreted her, he felt better. Nonetheless, Mr. S.
still remains very fragile and financial and familial concerns can quickly
bring back thoughts of death and suicide. Mr. S. minimized this interaction
afterwards, which is also worrisome as this may indicate a lack of insight into
his own fragility. Mr. S. remains in a locked unit in order to ensure he is in
a safe place if he again has episodes of wanting to die again. As well, he is
regularly refusing several aspects of treatment and believes that he does not
need to be in hospital, thus putting him at risk of leaving hospital without
permission.

[
46
]

Dr. Biskin explains that Mr. S. is still at high
risk of a suicide attempt if confronted with stressors:

In general,
Mr. S. continues to
have poor insight into the pattern that have led him to have frequent visits to
ER, multiple hospitalizations and suicide attempts
. He is not able to
describe the stressors is some cases and when he is able to describe them, he
simply states that things will be different in the future. He shows no signs of
changing the way he deals with stressors and,
in the absence of any
objective change, remains at extremely high risk of committing suicide when
stressors recur
.

(…)

He is not suicidal at present, but
is at very high risk of suicide if he experiences any stressors, and especially
if he does not have people to support him when he is in crisis.

Our
underlining

[
47
]

Dr. Biskin concludes that if Mr. S. is
authorized to return home at this time, it would place him at high risk:

In summary, Mr. S. continues to
pose a serious risk to his own life due to his diagnoses of major depressive
disorder, severe and in early partial remission, dependent personality
disorder, and benzodiazepine dependence. His history of non-compliance with
treatment and returning to the same environment and stressors that have triggered
many previous suicide attempts and suicidal thoughts prevent proper recovery.
In particular, the major risk is returning to his home environment as it is
highly stressful and has repeatedly been identified as the major factor leading
to suicidal behaviour. Mr. S. has consistently demonstrated an inability to
make changes in his home environment or to leave this environment, which puts
him at such high risk.

[
48
]

Under the circumstances, for the reasons exposed
by Dr. Biskin, the Court concludes that the mental condition of Mr. S. has
definite effect on his ability to consent to treatment and hospitalization.

[
49
]

The Court agrees with the petitioners that Mr. S.
is manifestly incapable of opposing, in a clear and in lighted manner, the
treatments which have been recommended in this case and which have been judged
absolutely necessary in light of his present state, and without restriction:

a)

he doesn’t understand the nature of his
psychiatric problems and explanations relative to the treatment plan envisaged;

b)

his illness impairs his ability to fully
comprehend the potential dangerousness of his delusions;

c)

his history of pervasive pattern of
discontinuing his medications renders necessary the forced treatment requested.

[
50
]

Mr. S. thinks he is in remission and can go
home. He does not realize the extend of his illness, the danger of going back
to his stressors and the importance of the treatment needed.

[
51
]

The treatment plan proposed by the Jewish
General Hospital medical team is in the best interest of Mr. S..

[
52
]

If Mr. S. cooperates, he should be out of the
intensive care closed unit in a short period. The transfer to a group home
should also be considered as soon as his condition improves and the space
becomes available.

[
53
]

The Hospital seeks an order for a period of 12
months from the present judgment. According to the evidence, this period is
reasonable.

[
54
]

It is obvious that if Mr. S. cooperates and if
his condition improves rapidly, the treating team might conclude for an earlier
return home.

[
55
]

For this to happen, Mr. S. will need the support
and understanding of his wife and all the members of his family.

FOR THESE
REASONS, THE COURT:

[
56
]

GRANTS
the
motion;

[
57
]

AUTORIZES
the Sir
Mortimer B. Davis – Jewish General Hospital to take the necessary measures in
order to treat Mr. S., despite his refusal, in the manner and according to the
following conditions :

•

The administration, during hospitalization and
out-patient follow-up, of medications as deemed appropriate by his treating
team; Mr. S. is currently prescribed:

-

Losartan;

-

Atenolol;

-

Atorvastatin;

-

Ativan;

-

Flomax;

-

Remeron;

-

Pioglitazone;

-

Cipralex;

-

Trazodone;

•

The administration, if necessary, of medication
to mitigate side effects;

•

Clinical investigations as necessary to monitor
the patient’s medical condition and medication level and/or effects;

•

Compliance with regular outpatient follow-up
appointments with a psychiatric treatment team of the Hospital;

•

Residing in a setting approved by the patient’s
treating team;

The whole for a period of 12 months from the present judgment, with
medications at a dosage which may be adjusted or modified by the treating
physician, according to the evolution of the clinical state of Mr. S., his
response to the aforementioned medication and according to the lowest possible
effective dosage;

[
58
]

ORDERS
Mr. S., to
submit to the treatment plan requested and
ORDERS
him to abide by the
instructions of his treating physician with respect to the control of this
state and the continuation of his outpatient treatment;

[
59
]

ORDERS
Mr. S., if
he does not comply with his out-patient treatment, be transported to the Sir
Mortimer B. Davis - Jewish General Hospital by ambulance or a peace officer,
upon request of his treating psychiatrist or any member of the treating team
and hospitalized, so that treatment may be resumed within the briefest delay,
for a period not exceeding 21 days, in order to prevent a psychotic relapse and
a dangerous behaviour;

[
60
]

ORDERS
the peace
officers to use the necessary force if Mr. S. refuses to comply with the
transportation in accordance with the order;

[
61
]

ORDERS
any
treating physician of Mr. S., to report on the evolution of his health every 6
months from the present judgment, to the Council of Physicians Dentists and
Pharmacists (CPDP) of the institution;

[
62
]

ORDERS
the Sir
Mortimer B. Davis – Jewish General Hospital, in the event of any conflict
between the treating psychiatrist and the CPDP of the institution, to notify
the Court immediately;

[
63
]

AUTHORIZES
any
other hospital or health institution where Mr. S. could be transferred to take
the necessary measures in order to treat him according to the conclusions of
the present judgment;

[
64
]

ORDERS
that the
judgment hereto be enforceable notwithstanding appeal;

[
65
]

WITHOUT COSTS.
